title: Servo: A Motor That Checks Its Work
description: Component lesson. A DC motor spins forever. A servo does something smarter: it goes exactly where you tell it, then holds — and knows if something pushes it off.

content.value: A DC motor is great at spinning continuously, but useless if you want a part to hold a precise angle — say, a sensor head aimed at exactly 45°. A servo solves that by wrapping a small DC motor in extra parts whose whole job is knowing exactly where the output shaft currently is, and correcting until it matches where you asked it to be.

Inside a servo: a small DC motor, a gear train that trades its speed for torque (you'll meet gear ratios properly later in this module), and — the key part — a potentiometer mechanically linked to the output shaft, which reports the shaft's actual current angle back to a tiny control board.

commanded angle  ---\
                      >  compare  --> error --> drive motor toward zero error
measured angle   ---/                              (potentiometer feedback)

That's a feedback loop: compare what's commanded to what's actually measured, and keep correcting until the difference (the error) is zero. It runs continuously, many times a second — which is exactly why a servo fights back if you push its horn away by hand.

content.title: 🎯 Command an angle
content.hint: Try 0°, then 180°, then somewhere in between. Watch for the small overshoot before it settles — that's the loop correcting itself.

content.value:
Part          SG90 micro servo
Range         0°–180°
Control       pulse-width signal (next lesson)
Torque        ≈ 1.8 kg·cm
Price         ≈ ₹120

This closed-loop idea — measure, compare, correct — is one of the most reused patterns in all of engineering, not just robotics. A thermostat, a cruise control, even your own hand reaching for a cup all run some version of the same loop.
Key takeaway: a servo is a motor plus a feedback loop — it measures its own position with a potentiometer, compares it to the commanded angle, and drives until the error is zero.

quiz.question: What tells a servo's control board where its output shaft currently is?
options: A potentiometer mechanically linked to the shaft
It doesn't know — servos run blind
quiz.explain: The potentiometer's reading is the "measured angle" half of the feedback loop — without it, there'd be nothing to compare the command against.

quiz.question: Why does a servo fight back if you push its horn away by hand?
options: The feedback loop detects the resulting error and keeps driving the motor to correct it
Servos are always locked rigid and can't be pushed
quiz.explain: Pushing the horn changes the measured angle, creating an error against the commanded angle — and the loop responds exactly as it's designed to.

quiz.question: What's the small overshoot you see when a servo settles onto a new angle?
options: The feedback loop correcting itself — it's part of how the loop behaves, not a bug
quiz.explain: A responsive feedback loop often overcorrects slightly before settling exactly on target — normal behaviour, not a fault.
